report:
**Conclusion: No.** The best current evidence indicates that saw palmetto (*Serenoa repens*) preparations do **not** meaningfully improve urinary symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) over placebo in the longer term.

A 2023 Cochrane review found **high-certainty evidence** of little to no difference in symptom scores at 12–17 months (mean IPSS difference 0.07; 95% CI −0.75 to 0.88; 898 participants) and no meaningful difference in quality of life. This is far below a clinically important benefit. [Cochrane](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001423_serenoa-repens-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia)

This agrees with a year-long randomized placebo-controlled trial, which found saw palmetto was not superior to placebo for urinary symptoms or objective BPH measures. [Trial report](https://escholarship.org/content/qt3d70w83q/qt3d70w83q.pdf) A further 72-week dose-escalation trial also showed no benefit—even at doses above usual use: symptom scores fell 2.2 points with saw palmetto versus 3.0 with placebo. [EurekAlert summary of the trial](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/668995)

The U.S. National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health similarly concludes that the large high-dose trial and Cochrane review found saw palmetto no more effective than placebo. [NCCIH](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/providers/digest/spotlight-on-saw-palmetto)

If urinary symptoms are bothersome, worsen, or include blood in urine, fever, pain, retention, or recurrent infections, seek clinical assessment rather than relying on saw palmetto.
